This paper introduces the TV-PAR model, a novel framework for modeling and forecasting the temporal dynamic dependencies within multivariate count data. We demonstrate that parametric autoregressive models, whether univariate or multivariate, possess sufficient expressive power to capture the first-order temporal dependencies observed in practical applications. Building on this insight, we propose a new method that utilizes a time-varying vector auto regression moving average component to account for any remaining residual temporal dependencies. Empirical analysis based on univariate and multivariate count data from telecommunications, finance, and healthcare illustrates the effectiveness of our approach. Furthermore, comparative experiments against existing methods highlight the forecasting superiority of our method. The utility of this framework extends beyond optimization; it serves scientific research by enabling the decomposition of temporal dependencies into static and dynamic components for in-depth investigation, and it offers a alternative to copula-based methods for capturing first-order temporal dependencies in the joint distribution. Our methodology also provides a robust solution for ensuring structural stability when conducting structural analysis through causal inference or structural decomposition. Finally, we establish the structural statistical properties of this model, including consistent and efficient estimation via maximum likelihood, and validate its use for structural analysis. Simulation studies and real-world data experiments collectively confirm the forecasting advantage of our method over alternatives and verify its structural and statistical properties. The proposed framework is applicable across various domains, particularly in economics and finance for economic and financial data analysis, and in operations research for count data related to supply chain disruptions, product returns, and machine failures. Open source code is available at https://github.com/Abhishek-1998/Temporal-Varying Poisson Auto Regression.

Although cosmic stars serve as an ideal reference standard for calibrating the radiometric response of aerosol measurements, they have historically been underutilized for satellite satellite comparisons due to the assumption that linear extrapolations from spaceborne spectrometers to narrow atmospheric bands would yield superior calibration methods. However, this approach has failed to deliver expected benefits, likely because of unaccounted uncertainties in stellar spectral energy distributions (SED) arising from atmospheric absorption, atmospheric variability, and photometric system mismatches. These factors introduce significant errors when calibrating atmospheric radiometric data via stellar photometry. While recent years have seen heightened interest in utilizing stellar variability for inter-satellite comparisons to detect drifts, these efforts have predominantly occurred outside formal operational workflows. We anticipate that upcoming hyperspectral instruments, such as the Hyperion sensor on the Japanese Hyperspectral Imager for the Global Observations of Pollution and nitrogen (HIGEPN) mission, will employ stellar variability for drift detection and detection-attribution. To support this, we must develop robust, efficient, and precise calibration techniques for airborne and spaceborne sensors using stellar variability, potentially leveraging machine learning. Furthermore, variable stars could play a crucial role in post-mission calibration for interplanetary missions, where direct calibration sources like the sun are inaccessible. This review examines recent progress in calibrating atmospheric gas observations from ground-based and spaceborne platforms using stellar photometry and its variability, offering a comprehensive summary of the necessary methodologies for implementing this technique in atmospheric science. Additionally, we will assess recent advancements in estimating aerosol optical depth (AOD) from satellite data to better utilize stellar photometry for calibration and detection/attribution analyses. Finally, we will explore how this method can be applied to refine global AOD products and identify spatial or temporal anomalies in individual satellite-derived AOD estimates. Although Markov Chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) methods have been extensively utilized to sample molecular conformational spaces, they often suffer from inefficient transitions between distinct local minima. In this study, we demonstrate that Langevin Dynamics (LD), an alternative approach, offers a robust and efficient alternative for exploring conformational spaces, particularly outperforming Metropolis-Hastings (MH) and Heat Bath (HB) algorithms for large biomolecules. Using a simple peptide as a test case, we observed that LD required approximately 20 times fewer steps than MH or HB to achieve the same level of sampling efficacy. Further analysis reveals that the efficacy of any Monte Carlo sampler is heavily dependent on the underlying proposal distribution's properties; specifically, the autocorrelation of physical velocities in LD directly influences the autocorrelation of conformational changes proposed by an equivalent MH algorithm. Leveraging this insight, we developed a novel MH variant called Velocity-Autocorrelation MH (VAMH), which matches LD sampling efficacy while being roughly 20 times faster per step. As a practical application, we employed LD to resolve topological ambiguities in Low Angle Neutron Scattering (LANS) data for the 550 kDa 70S ribosome, a task previously unsolved by standard Monte Carlo techniques like MH. Finally, we integrated LD with small-angle scattering (SAS) experiments to distinguish between alternative low-energy topological models of the 70S ribosome, validating our findings against cryo-EM data. Open-source implementations of both LD and VAMH for AMBER and CHARMM force fields, suitable for use with various molecular simulation packages, are available at https://github.com/shivank99/LDsample. Additionally, the specific application to 70S ribosome Low Angle Neutron Scattering (LANS) data is detailed in a companion paper by the same authors.

Current evaluations of systems generating natural language from images rely on comparing outputs against human references, utilizing metrics that ideally measure the semantic equivalence between the two. However, leveraging human references to evaluate automatic image description tools, particularly in industrial settings, may not always be feasible or optimal. In this work, we explore the possibility of assessing these systems without directly using human comments, by instead exploiting the references to define a semantic similarity metric between image captions and professional evaluations from users who are not experts in the specific domain where the tool is applied. We propose a pipeline that employs two neural networks: a task-specific classifier and a sentence encoder, to derive such a metric. This metric was derived by analyzing over 150,000 Flickr images paired with both user-generated comments and corresponding ground truth descriptions. When tested on two standard datasets, this approach achieved performance comparable to state-of-the-art metrics like BLEU, BLEURT, and BAT. Furthermore, as evidenced by heatmaps and statistical analyses, the metric correlates strongly with user ratings and effectively discriminates between image descriptions that align with user expectations and those that do not. The underlying neural network architectures and code are accessible at https://github.com/sergeykivinskyy/semanticsim. We anticipate that this metric will prove particularly valuable for industry professionals responsible for selecting appropriate image description tools and for guiding their optimization. Additionally, this work provides insights into suitable metrics for competitions where outputs are evaluated by human referees rather than automated means. Ultimately, the proposed metric serves as a valuable resource for researchers aiming to advance the field of image description.

Municipal and industrial gas fires are susceptible to instabilities driven by ambient turbulence or acoustic waves, potentially leading to intense pulsating flames that increase radiative heat flux and pose significant safety risks. Simulating these fires to investigate their response to acoustic forcing presents a significant challenge, particularly when employing Large Eddy Simulation (LES) within a high-fidelity reactive LES framework. This study applies an active flame model to a reactive LES model to evaluate the feasibility of simulating turbulent jet fires exposed to acoustic waves linearly. First, a reactive LES model was configured to represent a MAFF (Manhattan Acoustic Forcing Facility) test, demonstrating that planar acoustic waves generated by opposing line arrays did not reach the source region due to reflections from upstream boundaries. Subsequently, an identical test was simulated using the linearized reactive LES approach, accurately reproducing the desired acoustic excitation. Finally, a J-20 MAFF configuration was simulated in two configurations: initially with the straightforward reactive LES setup, which failed to generate the intended acoustic oscillations, and secondly with the linearized reactive LES method, successfully capturing the target oscillatory behavior. These results confirm that simulating jet fires reacting to acoustic forcing via directly numerical methods demands extremely fine spatial and temporal resolutions. Conversely, the linearized reactive LES approach effectively modeled the interaction between a turbulent jet fire and incident acoustic waves, offering a promising tool for resolving small-scale structures induced by acoustic excitation in future simulations. This paper provides an overview of the most significant rare processes detectable at proton-proton colliders, beginning with a summary of LHC experimental capabilities for analyzing specific final states. It then details the primary processes responsible for producing the WZ, ZZ, and tZ(t)() systems, as well as other relevant contributions. Finally, we present current limits on various diphoton + jet + E_T missing events and outline promising directions for future research. These rare processes offer ideal laboratories for investigating physics within the Standard Model at high energies and for searching for new phenomena, serving as ideal test cases for future high-luminance colliders. At future hadron machines, the priority will shift from measuring cross-sections to uncovering novel physics; for instance, the High-Luminosity LHC will enhance sensitivity to new resonances by a factor of ten, and the High-Energy HL-LHC could potentially discover new particles with masses up to 4.5 times that of the Higgs boson. At fixed-target baryon-baryon colliders like the AFTER@LHC experiment, new resonances will be produced on purpose, on-shell, with high cross-sections. This document also offers an overview of searches for exotic hadrons at the LHC, highlighting recent findings and future prospects. Fortunately, events with exactly two or zero jets and missing transverse energy will receive dedicated attention at baryon-baryon colliders, as these final states will be ideal for searching for new particles. First, we derive a general formula for the recurrence period of an SMBH transient, highlighting its dependence on the post-flare slope of the light curve and the corresponding timescale. Second, we analyze the variability characteristics of X-ray transients from neutron star (NS) systems, proposing a method to employ these events to detect NS activity in gas-dominant stellar systems around the GC-SMBH. Finally, we apply this approach to investigate the properties of the GC quiescent X-ray binaries. Although this strategy is contingent upon observing NS transients in the GC, its utility extends beyond this specific goal; the derivation of the general recurrence period formula for such events may prove valuable for similar searches in external galaxies. Furthermore, if NS transients are detected in the GC by future observations, this could provide critical insights into the mass and gravitational influence of the "dynamical mass gap" objects orbiting the GC-SMBH. Ultimately, if variable fading times can be employed to identify SMBH transients in the GC and other galaxies, it would offer an effective method for identifying low-mass SMBHs in extragalactic systems. We conclude with suggestions for future research in this area. This work was not guided by observations from the LIGO/Virgo/KAGRA gravitational wave detectors. High-performance applications frequently exceed the throughput capabilities of current CPUs, a limitation we address by introducing HyperDegrade. This technique enables programs that surpass CPU speed limits to run faster by executing selected computational kernels at higher frequencies using hardware voltage frequency scaling (VFS). HyperDegrade dynamically balances workload execution speeds and performance through an online, iterative algorithm that optimizes overall performance without missing deadlines. Our extensive evaluations demonstrate that HyperDegrade outperforms existing real-time scheduling methods, meeting all deadlines while achieving up to 2.7x greater performance gain than state-of-the-art workload schedulers. Furthermore, our results confirm that HyperDegrade surpasses theoretical performance limits established by static workloads. These findings indicate that workloads utilizing HyperDegrade can exceed the performance gains possible with static voltage frequency scaling (e.g., running all workloads at maximum frequency), particularly when workloads are heterogeneous and have varying performance requirements at different frequencies. To support these evaluations, we released the open-source system "Voltnomist," which dynamically prioritizes workloads executing at frequencies above their normal operating points. Source code for both HyperDegrade and Voltnomist is accessible at https://github.com/ntucci/HyperDegrade and https://github.com/ntucci/Voltnomist, respectively.

This study examines simple global atmospheric circulation patterns in a 2D, viscous, rotating, tidally locked atmosphere subject to differential heating between a hot star and cool planet. This study addresses a spurious vertical bias observed in vector magnetic field data generated by the INVMC inversion model when applied to SunPM solar view imaging. When contextualized against the solar view captured by SunPM, this bias represents a measurement error arising from the inversion of vector fields from a single viewpoint. Such "spike-like" artifacts are a known consequence of solving vector fields from limited viewing angles, specifically polarized imaging, when specific assumptions about the magnetic field distribution are made. While this bias does not invalidate the reconstructed vector fields for the SunPM view when analyzed in local coordinates, it creates significant issues when the data is examined in global coordinates or when compared with views from other telescopes. To mitigate this bias for SunPM views, we modified the inversion process using a regularizer that penalizes this specific spurious behavior. We evaluated the effectiveness of this approach by comparing the corrected SunPM views (after application of the correction) with concurrent views from the Beltstrip Imager on the GoTelescope in Germany, leveraging a global optimization method to find the best-matching global coordinates. The results indicate that the bias in the original SunPM views aligns precisely with the magnetic field distributions in the visible vertical axis derived from the GoTelescope views, and our correction successfully mitigated this discrepancy. Although this work focuses specifically on the bias present in SunPM views, the underlying issues, causes, and proposed solutions are applicable to similar problems in other vector magnetic field data obtained from single-view telescopes. Implementing this correction has the potential to enhance data utility for projects utilizing SunPM views, such as operational forecasts (e.g., WOlFi), scientific investigations (particularly those involving global analysis or comparing multi-telescope views), and machine learning initiatives (for training models on SunPM views). Furthermore, this research highlights the necessity of carefully selecting regularizers in non-linear inversion methods and offers guidance for selecting appropriate regularizers in similar contexts. Although significant advancements have been made in deep learning loss functions over the past few years, there remains no consensus on their optimal selection for specific tasks or datasets. This study conducts extensive experiments to evaluate various loss functions across three architectures: fully connected networks, convolutional neural networks, and transformers. The evaluation covers 21 different datasets, ranging from balanced to highly imbalanced datasets with 10 to 100+ classes. The comparative analysis focuses on two primary metrics: Area Under the Receiver Operating Characteristic Curve (AUC-ROC) and F1-score. Our findings indicate that for highly imbalanced datasets, Cross Entropy with Sampling (CEs) consistently outperforms standard Cross Entropy (CE) and other loss functions when evaluated by AUC-ROC. Conversely, when using the F1-score as the metric, the Weighted Cross Entropy (WCE) loss is always superior to CEs. These results suggest that while sampling-based approaches like CEs effectively utilize underrepresented samples in an AUC-ROC context, they may still assign lower weights to those same samples within an F1-score framework, whereas the weighting mechanism in WCE more effectively prioritizes them to improve classification accuracy. Additionally, we observe that network complexity, measured by the count of learnable parameters, does not significantly impact the final model's performance. Finally, regarding optimization algorithms, Adam or its variants are not necessarily superior to stochastic gradient descent with momentum (SGD+M) or other optimizers; the best choice depends entirely on the specific dataset and loss function combination. To support these conclusions, we release a comprehensive dataset of 21 widely used datasets along with their corresponding loss curves and other performance statistics, available at https://github.com/Aniruddha-1/LFComparison. We introduce ATOMIC, a massive atlas of machine common knowledge structured as if-then reasoning traces. This resource compiles structured descriptions of commonly-sense inferences from extensive knowledge bases, including ConceptNet, CN-DB, YAGO3, YAGO-C, and FreebaseR20.14. By organizing these descriptions into a uniform format, we enable the retrieval of implicit knowledge triggers alongside their corresponding inferences. Furthermore, this uniform structure facilitates the generation of common-sense inferences by external systems. To populate the atlas, we developed an automatic extraction pipeline that leverages structured data and natural language processing over textual knowledge bases. Additionally, we developed a toolkit for visually rendering inferences to support human analysis and verification. Evaluations demonstrate that the pipeline successfully retrieves a substantial number of implicit knowledge triggers and their associated inferences from various knowledge bases. Benchmark tests against existing datasets reveal that inferences retrieved via ATOMIC's if-then reasoning formulation achieve higher accuracy than those retrieved using alternative methods. Finally, we conducted user studies to assess the atlas's utility for tasks such as knowledge completion, completion justification, and inference generation. These evaluations, along with benchmarks, indicate that deep neural networks can be trained on ATOMIC to perform reasoning over inputs defined by implicit knowledge triggers. Experiments show that models trained on ATOMIC surpass state-of-the-art approaches on standard benchmarks for detecting inferential relations and performing inference. The source code and data for ATOMIC are accessible at https://github.com/ATOMIC-Atlas/ATOMIC.

Metric dimension, a concept within discrete geometry, extends the traditional measure of dimension (defined as $d$) to graphs, yielding values of at least $d$. Consequently, the metric dimension of any graph $G$ adhering to the distance constraint $d(G) \leq k$ is inherently bounded by $k$. Given that computing the metric dimension is NP-hard, determining it for a specific graph remains a challenging task. In this work, we introduce the notion of metric dimension under a restricted distance function, denoted by $d_k$, where measurements are capped at $k$. Correspondingly, we define the metric dimension as $\dim_k(G)$ based on this restricted distance function $d_k$. We examine several standard graphs to clarify how $\dim_k(G)$ varies with $k$ for a fixed structure $G$. Furthermore, for specific graphs, we derive exact values of $\dim_k(G)$ without relying on the traditional dimension $d(G)$. Our analysis covers paths, cycles, spiders, and a broad class of graphs known as graphs of order $n$ composed of a path $P_r$ and a star $K_{1,s}$, where $r + s = n - 1$. We also investigate the extremal problem concerning the order of graphs that possess a given $\dim_k(G)$ value. Additionally, we establish the relationship between $\dim_1(G)$ and the diameter of $G$, and similarly link $\dim_2(G)$ with the number of diametral edges in $G$. All discussions pertain to simple, connected, undirected graphs. Our findings suggest that $\dim_k(G)$ serves as a meaningful invariant, potentially offering significant utility in network theory. Regarding nomenclature, we utilize $w(D)$ to represent the weight of a function $D: V(G) \rightarrow \{1,0\}$, and $N(k)$ (for $k \geq 1$) to denote the maximum order of a graph $G$ such that $\dim_k(G) = 2$. Finally, the symbol $[a_1,a_2,\ldots,a_n]$ signifies the vector $(a_1,a_2,\ldots,a_n)$.

Cardiac auscultation serves as a critical point-of-care technique for detecting heart conditions, yet the development of intelligent auscultation systems (CAA) remains hindered by the high variability of acoustic signals. This variability stems from physiological factors, such as the location and intensity of sounds during auscultation, as well as extraneous additive noise introduced by the recording environment and device. Although deep learning approaches have been widely adopted to address this variability in cardiac sound classification, they often lack robustness against acoustic noise variations. In contrast, image recognition methods have successfully utilized deformation-based techniques to handle invariance to both location and noise. However, applying these strategies to cardiac sounds is challenging due to the difficulty in visually observing noise-related deformations and the scarcity of existing de-noising models suitable for cardiac data. To overcome these obstacles, we propose a novel end-to-end architecture that integrates a data-driven De-noising Network (DeNet) with a Convolutional Deformation Network (DiNet) specifically designed for heart sound categorization. Our framework uniquely combines a DeNet with a DI-Net (Inverted DI-Net) in an end-to-end configuration to mitigate both location and additive noise variations. Experimental results from public datasets demonstrate that this approach surpasses current state-of-the-art methods. Furthermore, the model exhibits significant robustness when tested under simulated real-world noise conditions. The source code for this project is accessible at: https://github.com/AbdulKhaleque1997/ASDnet. We anticipate that this architecture will prove valuable for clinical applications, particularly in point-of-care scenarios involving noisy environments or when using low-cost acoustic recording devices. Ultimately, such solutions could facilitate tele-medicine initiatives and provide a data-driven alternative to manual analysis by cardiologists for categorizing heart sound sounds into normal or abnormal categories. Although significant progress has been made in developing models to simulate and forecast the progression of infections during the current SARS-CoV-2 epidemic, existing frameworks lack the necessary flexibility and generality. This work advocates for a unified, compartmental modeling approach capable of simulating both classic and innovative outbreak investigations, including backtracking studies, real-time epidemic forecasts, and the evaluation of epidemiological interventions and hypotheses during the current SARS-CoV-2 outbreak. While no single general-purpose model can replace the specialized tools required for certain tasks—such as estimating biological parameters like basic and effective reproductive rates, or analyzing genetic and contact tracing data—a flexible central model can integrate with these specialized methods to form a comprehensive statistical framework. Furthermore, such a model can be simulated using various techniques, ranging from simple simulation-based inference to advanced simulation-based approaches like causal inference, optimal experimental design, and game theory to guide epidemiological studies and interventions. Ultimately, this unified framework can also be leveraged for counterfactual simulations to assess the impact of interventions and strategic decisions. Demonstrating this concept in the context of the current SARS-CoV-2 epidemic, we constructed a flexible compartmental model and connected it with diverse statistical methods and data sources to simulate classic studies and investigative activities occurring globally. As the SARS-CoV-2 epidemic evolves into a longer-term challenge, this flexible framework can be adapted to investigate new issues and emerging research queries. Although the volume of fake news on social media has recently decreased due to intensified monitoring by tech giants, governments, and NGOs, the development of effective detection systems remains essential for identifying potential misinformation. To validate MetaUFN, we created a novel dataset termed MetaMultilingual, which includes 1,800 articles in English, Hindi, and Tamil, with manual annotations for both real and fake classifications. Segmentation networks trained on medical images are frequently compromised by adversarial lesions, small pixel alterations that remain undetectable to humans yet cause misclassification. These lesions pose a significant challenge for clinical applications, as their existence undermines the reliability of automated medical image analysis. Although prior research has successfully introduced adversarial lesions, generating them in clinically plausible locations remains difficult. This paper presents a novel framework for creating lesional and counter-lesional adversarial perturbations in brain MRI scans through a progressive approach. First, the framework generates global adversarial perturbations using a standard convolutional neural network (CNN). These initially unrealistic lesional and non-lesional changes then serve as conditions for an variational auto-encoder (VAE), which refines the perturbations to produce clinically feasible adversarial lesions while preserving segmentation accuracy on global regions. Experiments conducted on two brain MRI datasets—ADNI and HUAT—demonstrate that these lesional and counter-lesional perturbations effectively fool both supervised and unsupervised segmentation models. Furthermore, the generated lesions align closely with ground truth lesional and non-lesional areas, as confirmed by visual inspection and quantitative metrics. The source code and dataset are accessible at: https://github.com/Aniruddha-1997/ProgressiveVAE. Readers may contact the corresponding author at aniruddha.s@uwaterloo.ca. The proposed method offers a valuable tool for assessing the robustness of cerebral lesion segmentation networks against adversarial attacks and provides a platform for further investigation into the characteristics of lesional and non-lesional adversarial perturbations in brain MRI data. Ultimately, this framework could support the development of new models capable of distinguishing between lesional and non-lesional adversarial lesions, with potential applications in explaining classification decisions and enhancing the overall security of brain MRI segmentation systems. Feature extraction (FE) serves as a pivotal preprocessing step in tasks like classification and regression, finding extensive application across domains including bioinformatics, chemistry, and linguistics to facilitate downstream comparative learning (CL) tasks. Given the high dimensionality of raw data in these fields, FE is essential for making such datasets manageable. Although many heuristic-based methods have been developed, they lack theoretical grounding and often yield suboptimal results. In contrast, unsupervised learning approaches grounded in CL have recently emerged; however, existing literature employs a fragmented collection of disparate techniques to construct end-to-end neural network models. This paper introduces a unified structure for unsupervised feature extraction via comparative learning, demonstrating its superiority over both heuristic and prior unsupervised methods through extensive experiments. These tests cover three large-scale linguistic datasets and two bioinformatics datasets, utilizing state-of-the-art CL neural network architectures. The proposed framework is highly versatile, accommodating various FE dimensions, data types (continuous or one-hot encoded), and task types (one-to-one, one-to-many, or many-to-many CL). Furthermore, the approach requires no manual feature engineering, as the feature space is defined by the network structure itself. Ultimately, this unified structure is easily adaptable to other domains such as chemistry and bioinformatics, provided the corresponding one-hot encoding tables are established. The implementation details are available at: https://github.com/AbdelwahabElshafey/Unified_FE_CS.

Elevated order methods, first introduced by Bunch and Hanchen in 1977 and later expanded by Pan in 1988, offer an iterative approach to matrix inversion that achieves a complexity of $O(n^{log_2(17)}) \approx n^{2.71}$. This paper generalizes these elevated order techniques and introduces a new framework called "successive elevated order inversion." Within this framework, the order of inversion is successively doubled at each iteration. Theoretical analysis confirms that successive elevated order inversion maintains numerical stability, and empirical results support this claim. Additionally, the method benefits from effective parallelization, making it ideal for deployment on GPUs. These advantages position successive elevated order inversion as a superior alternative to standard approaches for high-dimensional low-rank matrix inversion. When integrated with standard inversion techniques, it enables significant reductions in both computational complexity and memory usage for large-scale matrix inversions. Practical applications demonstrate that this method outperforms state-of-the-art libraries, including MAGMA and MKL, for matrices exceeding 10,000 dimensions. Furthermore, when combined with common deep learning architectures, successive elevated order inversion facilitates the inversion of massive matrices that surpass current feasibility limits, as illustrated by a concrete example in this work. Despite these benefits, it is important to note that for lower-dimensional matrices, the method may underperform compared to established techniques. The objective of a contextual learning agent is to minimize total regret over time by leveraging a contextual linear learner to estimate the optimal policy. We developed a 3D hydrodynamical simulation to investigate how dust accumulation influences the excitation and growth of the vertical shear instability (VSI) in the outer regions of protoplanetary disks. Our results indicate that while gas dynamics tend to localize dust settling at pressure bumps, even minor dust accumulation within VSI-active zones significantly amplifies gravitational instabilities. In simulations featuring both VSI and dust, this interaction caused the vertical scale height to increase by a factor of two relative to VSI-only simulations without dust. Furthermore, we observed that dust accumulation preferentially occurs near the midplane within regions experiencing strong vertical shear. Ultimately, our findings suggest that the coexistence of dust and VSI could offer a mechanism for creating step-like structures in observed outer disk structures, such as those seen in HL Tau. Additionally, this mechanism may help concentrate dust at the boundaries of other protoplanetary disks exhibiting prominent midplane emission, including AS 209 and SA 209/210. These conclusions hold true even when dust experiences significant radiative cooling or sublimates due to compression; in such scenarios, structural changes still manifest at the midplane edges of regions where gas temperatures exceed the dust's sublimation temperature. Simulations conducted with cooling laws based on Ossomoff wavelengths align closely with those using fixed temperature profiles, supporting the notion that OSSOMOFF cooling becomes negligible in the low-density outer regions of protoplanetary disks. This study also clarifies the interplay between VSI-driven turbulence and dust settling, revealing that VSI turbulence is more effective than previously understood. Finally, we discuss how these results relate to the formation of dust traps and compare our findings with direct imaging observations. This study introduces Random Stroll Learning (RSL), a technique enabling clients with limited data ranges to acquire knowledge from external data ranges in Federated Learning (FL). Random walks (RW) are ideally suited for bridging data gaps, yet existing RW methods like Degree-based RW (D-RW) and Betweenness-based RW (B-RW) fail to access data outside their specific ranges. We propose a new approach, Random Point-based Stroll (P-RSL), which generates walks targeting underutilized data regions. Extensive simulations demonstrate that RSL effectively compensates for data deficiencies, outperforming standard logistic regression and conventional RW methods such as D-RW and B-RW on both synthetic and real-world datasets. Furthermore, RSL shows significant promise in medical applications, enabling access to medical data beyond its native scope. Simulations also confirm that RSL accelerates convergence in gradient-descent-based models, reducing the iterations required for other algorithms to match RSL's learning speed. Finally, we evaluated an educational dataset from India's government school system, revealing that prior to RSL, learning from data outside its range was unfeasible; afterward, students gained exposure to such data, and teachers could engage in discussions about it. These findings indicate that RSL can help develop more equitable education systems by allowing students and educators to learn from and discuss data beyond their local environments. The source code is available at: https://github.com/Abhishek-1999/RSL-LE.

Consistency regularization is a prominent method in unsupervised learning that aims to align predictions from multiple neural networks or across different data augmentations. Experimental results demonstrate that the proposed technique outperforms existing methods on both datasets. Furthermore, the utility of image segmentation as a task is confirmed by the model's ability to generate high-quality outputs even from unlabeled samples. We demonstrate genuine nonlocal effects stemming from single-particle entangerness, specifically realizing single-particle steering. This occurs when a genuinely nonlocal resource, namely single-particle entangerness, is employed. We confirm this experimentally using orbital angular momentum entangerness in a delayed single-particle setup. Additionally, we observe this phenomenon with spatial entangerness in a setup involving two spatial modes, and we predict that it can also arise from temporal entangerness in a bipartite configuration created by splitting a pulse into two time bins. These findings indicate that "spatial" and "temporal" modes exhibit analogous nonlocal characteristics, mirroring the equivalence between spatial and single-particle entangerness. Furthermore, as summarized by the Bell inequality violated in single-particle steering, these results imply that "time" can exhibit nonlocal behavior in the context of temporal steering within a delayed single-pulse arrangement. Finally, we establish that genuine nonlocal effects from single-particle entangerness can be utilized for information expansion via single-particle steering, achieving this through remote preparation of a Bessel function mode that possesses infinite dimensions. This process expands information content within a specific quantum communication task, characterized by a Bayes criterion that generalizes the violation of a Bell inequality for fairness in protocol comparison. We conclude by highlighting additional genuine nonlocal effects of single-particle entangerness that remain unexplored and by proposing information expansion protocols based on temporal steering.

Although Long short-term memory (LSTM) networks deliver high recognition accuracy in speech and video analysis, their substantial memory requirements and computational complexities restrict their practical application in resource-constrained environments like mobile devices and video gateways. The approach begins with a hierarchical Tucker tensor decomposition (TTD) of the weight matrices, followed by a hardware architecture for an image recognition processor based on this decomposition. Subsequently, they propose space-time TTD, which jointly decomposes weight matrices and one-hot encoded input vectors to further reduce memory needs and enhance energy efficiency. Building on this, they developed a specialized hardware architecture for input encoding and an associated LSTM network co-design strategy. Validation through trace-driven simulation and hardware emulation demonstrates that their co-design achieves significant reductions in energy consumption and memory usage compared to traditional methods. Specifically, a 72-kilometer highway segment video identification architecture utilizing this co-design was implemented on FPGA, requiring 53.1% less energy and 75.7% less memory than a comparable architecture using standard weight matrices on the same hardware platform. Finally, a real-time LSTM video identification architecture based on the proposed method and hardware configuration was designed and realized on FPGA for a video gateway, confirming the feasibility of processing video streams in real time on such hardware. The proposed method and architecture have been successfully applied to an actual video gateway, effectively identifying suspicious events and alerting security personnel. Although discourse markers (DMs) play a crucial role in human communication, their potential in building robust machine-readable metadata for digital libraries remains largely untapped. While deep learning methods have recently attempted to predict DMs from text using task-specific models or by integrating them with downstream goals like classification, these approaches do not guarantee accurate identification. Furthermore, existing discourse theory lacks computational resources necessary for verifying the appropriateness of detected markers regarding their intended semantic and pragmatic roles. To address these challenges, we present DiscSense, an system that automatically suggests and verifies the correct labeling and discourse functions of potential DMs within documents. Applying this tool to Wikipedia articles demonstrates that nearly 20% of the roughly 8000 non-anaphoric markers require function label changes to align with their actual usage, and significant revisions are also necessary for ensuring local coherence. These findings offer a set of guidelines for refining DM functions within formal theories. Additionally, by assigning uniform labels to discourse functions across languages, DiscEnable facilitates cross-lingual comparison and learning, a feature particularly valuable for low-resource languages. Ultimately, by automatically assigning DM functions to texts, this system serves as a valuable linguistic resource for both computational and human linguistic research, and as a tool for enhancing metadata in digital libraries to support discourse-based text processing and retrieval. This study presents a relativistic hydrodynamic theory of Josephson solitons (y--shiba--rusin states) to analyze Magnetic Spin Solitons (MSS) formed by an Mn adatom and Mn dimers on the Nb(110) surface. Through a relativistic hydrodynamic formulation of the wave equation for Yu--shiba--rusin states, we derived a new initial principles model (RIP) based on conservation laws of mass, momentum, and energy. Within the RIP model, we determined the exact analytical expressions for the transverse longitudinal energy $E_{\parallel}$, defined as the energy required to create an MSS of width $W$ along the Nb(110) surface. Our results indicate that in the massive sine--Gordon (sG) approximation, the energy equation for $E_{\parallel}$ yields two distinct analytical solutions for the width $W$: a stable solution ($W_s$) and an unstable solution ($W_u$). Going beyond the sG approximation, we employed the exact initial principles RIP model to calculate the energy barrier $\Delta U$ necessary for creating an intermediate MSS of width $W_{\rm int}$ ($W_s < W_{\rm int} < W_u$) during the transition from the stable to unstable configuration. This study examines the existence of invariant curves defined by $y = \lambda x^{\alpha} + h(x)$ within the phase plane of fractional-order systems. We demonstrate that such curves cannot exist when an integer-order term of at least quadratic degree is present in one of the variables. Leveraging this finding, we identify and rule out specific invariant surfaces in three-dimensional fractional-order systems. These results offer significant insights for qualifying dynamical models, particularly in applications involving biological and chemical processes. Notably, these conclusions are purely mathematical and hold true for all real positive values of the fractional order $\alpha$, regardless of whether the sum of system degrees of freedom exceeds the available dimension. Consequently, these outcomes correct erroneous claims of biological significance found in recent literature regarding biological models formulated as systems with a total degree of homogeneity greater than three. Finally, we generalize these results to provide a criterion for the nonexistence of invariant surfaces in various classes of three-dimensional fractional-order systems.
